title: Treaty Promises and Implementation in Alberta
intro: What was won at the councils and what went missing from the page. Block A evidence checkpoint.

terms.def: The 1876 wins Cree negotiators fought for: aid in pestilence or famine, and a medicine chest at each Indian Agent's house, later growing into health coverage.

body: Treaty Six shows both the bargaining and the cost. Facing buffalo decline, Cree negotiators won aid in pestilence or famine plus the medicine chest clause. Yet written texts omitted spoken commitments, and not every group living in an area was included when treaties were first written, which is why questions 32-34 demand the textbook's exact Alberta details.

Block A checkpoint. Before moving on, you should be able to explain oral tradition's four threads, the Dene claim to nationhood, the collective logic of rights, the holistic lens, one early treaty, the Proclamation's double edge, the numbered-treaty understanding gap, and the Treaty Six concessions.

Treaty Six also teaches bargaining under pressure. With the buffalo collapsing, Cree negotiators converted desperation into two lasting wins, and the medicine-chest clause outgrew its origins: a promise of one chest at each agent's house became the ancestor of universal health coverage for treaty First Nations. Concessions compound across generations, for both sides.

What went missing matters as much as what was written. Oral promises stayed out of the texts, and groups living in treaty areas but absent from the councils found themselves excluded from the terms. Implementation questions always ask two things: what the paper says, and who was never at the table.

example.title: Answer with the page open
example.text: Questions 32-34 ask for a Treaty One verbal promise left out of writing, two Treaty Six concessions, and which groups were excluded. These need textbook pages 29-35 verbatim detail, so answer them with the chapter open rather than from memory.

check.prompt: What did Cree negotiators win at Treaty Six, and what did it become?
check.sample: Sample response: famine and pestilence aid plus a medicine chest at each agent's house, a clause that later grew into universal health coverage for treaty First Nations.

title: Geography, Resources, and Forms of Governance
intro: How land shaped six ways of life and rule. Questions 37-38 are answered in this lesson — your writing saves here.

terms.def: How a people organizes leadership, law, and decisions. Traditional forms answered to people's needs and the land that fed them.
The challenges and resources of a region, such as game, fish, timber, and climate, that shaped each culture's way of life.

body: Question 37 asks for six regions and, for each, the environmental challenges and the resources that shaped lives and culture: Pacific Northwest, Plateau, Plains, Eastern Woodlands, Subarctic, and Arctic. Work region by region from textbook pages 36-44, pairing each challenge with its resource before moving on.

Forms of governance grew from the same ground. Care for the land was built into rule: one technique was controlled burning, deliberately set fires that increased the diversity and productivity of animals and plants, guided by generations of observation passed down through oral tradition.

The mechanism is worth understanding, because the questions ask what burns did, not just that they happened. Fire clears choking undergrowth, ash nutrients enrich the soil, and regenerating areas draw more abundant game and plant life. Knowing that fire renews, leaders could schedule burns the way a treasurer schedules spending: deliberately, for future yield.

Environment shaped culture beyond food. Each region's challenges, cold, distance, flood, predator, set which skills, materials, and seasonal rounds a people developed, and those rounds set where councils met, when laws were renewed, and who led. Geography is the first chapter of every governance story in this block.

example.title: See it in the questions
example.text: Build the question 37 table with all six regions and both fields. Question 38 asks for two traditional Alberta meeting places from the same pages; answer it with the chapter open.

check.prompt: How did controlled burning show governance caring for the land?
check.sample: Sample response: deliberately set fires renewed game and plant life, with ash nutrients enriching regrowth, applying generations of observed knowledge to feed the people.

title: Land, Law, and Knowledge in Community Accounts
intro: Law carried in ceremony, story, and societies. Questions 35-36 and 39-43 are answered in this lesson — your writing saves here.

terms.def: Community institutions whose rules made up the rules of governance. Wolf Leg describes them as law libraries, with people as walking files of lived experience.
Obligations learned through story and ceremony, renewed when people gather, binding how they treat one another and the land.

body: Governance always responded to people's needs. People were reminded of the Creator's laws through story and ceremony, and inside the living circle stood Societies. Wolf Leg calls these Societies law libraries: the people are walking files recording lived experience, and their rules make up the rules of governance and of land itself.

A caution from the blueprint: question 35's pipe symbolism needs the textbook's exact account on pages 36-44, because retellings confuse the stem and the stone. Read those pages directly for questions 35-36 rather than trusting memory, and do the same for the uses of controlled burning in question 39.

Wolf Leg's image deserves a slow read. Walking files means law lived in experienced people, not archives: a dispute went to someone who had lived the precedent. Renewal through ceremony meant law stayed current, re-consented by each generation rather than frozen at enactment. That is a complete legal theory in three moves: storage, retrieval, renewal.

Pipe ceremonies sealed agreements the way signatures seal contracts, which is why smoking together at a council was law-making, not hospitality. The sacred weight is exactly what made later broken promises a violation of oath rather than a mere policy change.

example.title: Worked reading
example.text: When the textbook quotes Wolf Leg, first name the speaker and setting, then quote the law-library line, then explain in your own words what it claims about where law lives.

check.prompt: What does it mean to call Societies law libraries?
check.sample: Sample response: the Societies' rules were the community's laws, carried by people as lived experience and renewed in ceremony rather than written in books.
